The paper applies the method of moments to solve the electromagnetic scattering from dielectric/magnetic coated perfect conductors with arbitrary geometries.
The governing equations are derived using the equivalence principle and the dyadic formulation of Huygens' principle.

Triangular patch modeling is used to discretize the boundary surfaces, and the method of moments with a bi-triangular subdomain basis is used to convert the integro-differential equations into a matrix equation.
Radar cross section measurements were made on various coated and uncoated square aluminum plates at 3 GHz and 6 GHz to validate the theoretical predictions.
The coatings considered may have any arbitrary complex permittivity and/or permeability, and the governing equations are derived for both completely coated and partially coated perfect conductors.
The paper discusses the concepts for generalizing the approach to handle multi-layered coatings, both completely enclosing and partially enclosing the perfect conductor.
Geometrical optics fails to accurately predict the radar cross section near discontinuities such as edges, and it predicts an infinite RCS for flat or singly curved surfaces.

Physical optics uses a geometrical optics approximation of the fields induced on the body surface and integrates the induced fields to obtain the scattered field, which can better handle non-conducting and conducting surfaces.
The number of unknown surface current coefficients limits the size of target that can be handled using numerical methods like method of moments due to computer storage and processing limitations.
The method of moments approach is able to predict the radar cross section of coated perfect conductors with arbitrary geometries by solving the electromagnetic scattering problem.
Experimental measurements of radar cross section for various coated and uncoated square aluminum plates were compared to the theoretical predictions to validate the method.
The paper discusses the concepts for generalizing the approach to handle multi-layered coatings, which could have practical applications.
The low-frequency numerical techniques like method of moments and finite element method are used to complement the high-frequency asymptotic theories like geometrical optics and physical optics.
Hybrid methods have been developed that combine the strengths of the asymptotic and numerical techniques to handle different regions of a target.
Radar cross section prediction for coated objects is an important problem with many practical applications in areas like stealth technology and target identification.
